Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PA View image in fullscreen Streeting said that apart from on social media, being the first gay defence secretary had been ‘almost entirely unremarked upon’. Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PA Wes Streeting Wes Streeting describes ‘unbelievable volume’ of homophobic abuse since becoming defence secretary Streeting says role is chance to show strength and challenge stereotype that ‘persists in dark corners of internet’ Peter Walker Senior political correspondent Wed 26 Aug 2026 14.41 EDT First published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 14.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Wes Streeting has described receiving a mass of homophobic abuse since he was made defence secretary last month, while also saying his appointment had been welcomed by some in the Ministry of Defence (MoD) as a sign of change. Until 2000, gay men and lesbian women were banned from serving in the UK military, with about 200-plus personnel thrown out of the forces each year due to their sexuality – an estimate, as proper records were not kept. Streeting, who is the first out gay defence secretary, told the All Talk podcast hosted by Iain Dale: “I have experienced more online homophobia in the last three weeks than I have in my entire life. “Unbelievable volume – because people cannot cope with the idea that a gay person might lead the armed forces of the United Kingdom.” He went on: “And I have two things to say in response to that. One is, firstly, being the first openly gay defence secretary has been almost entirely unremarked upon in the media. “And I think, ‘Great, here we are in the third decade of the 21st century and it doesn’t matter, brilliant.’ But of course, online it matters to a lot of people. And I am proud of the fact that in my lifetime we’ve gone from gay people not being able to serve in the military to a gay defence secretary.” In 2024, Keir Starmer’s government set up the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme, under which personnel who were dismissed or discharged because of the ban in place from 1967 to 2000 can apply for payments of up to £70,000. Some MPs have since expressed concern at what they say is the slow pace of processing claims, while two veterans have begun legal action to challenge the fact that personnel who were forced to resign, rather than being dismissed or discharged, receive lower payments. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Streeting says Burnham government will prioritise military over other spending Read more Streeting told the podcast: “In my first week, someone in the MoD said to me, ‘As a gay man, I’m really proud that we have our first gay defence secretary. It means a lot to us who remember the bad old days.’ So I was quite touched by that. “As for the stuff online, I sort of think one of the wonderful things about today’s day and age is that we get to show just how strong we are. I see strength in all sorts of places in the LGBT community and people living normal, dull, suburban lives. It’s ordinary now being gay in Britain, which is brilliant. View image in fullscreen Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, last month unveiled plans to test US service personnel for their levels of testosterone. Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty “But I also look at service personnel, athletes now with some footballers coming out, we have got strength in numbers and we’ve got strength in confidence. It’s an opportunity for me to demonstrate strength in this role as well and to challenge the sort of stereotype that clearly persists in dark corners of the internet.” Part of Streeting’s role involves liaising with Pete Hegseth, the US’s more stereotypically traditional defence secretary, who last month unveiled plans to test US service personnel for their levels of testosterone. Like others in the Trump administration, Hegseth is a vehement opponent of equality and inclusion. Last year, he ordered the renaming of a US navy ship named in honour of Harvey Milk, the murdered navy veteran, gay rights activist and politician. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60q.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, A search and rescue operation involving boats and helicopters is now continuing in rough seas, Romania's authorities say By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 15 October 2026, 09:22 BST Updated 1 hour ago Seven of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a chemical tanker ablaze off Romania's coast on Thursday morning, naval authorities say. The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire. Romanian President NicuÈor Dan confirmed that the Wine Trader and another chemical tanker in the area, the Yara J, had both been struck by drones - the Yara J on Wednesday. The Wine Trader was empty of cargo at the time. Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port had been hit. It did not name the vessels. Overnight, a swarm of Russian drones was detected not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island. The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing. Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy. A search and rescue operation for the missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed. The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel. The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area. The Wine Trader tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 (05:00 GMT). Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader had been hit by two drones. The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked. This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened. The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state." Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region. The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area. Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports. On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable". Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine. A fire broke out on the Comoros-flagged Yara J late on Wednesday after being struck by a drone, but its crew - who are all reportedly safe - were able to douse the flames themselves. Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi. Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports. Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked. Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea. Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory . https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: People gathering in Oleshky before the joint-relief evacuation operation that will take them on a route through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory. Photograph: Facebook Official account of Kyrylo Budano/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People gathering in Oleshky before the joint-relief evacuation operation that will take them on a route through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory. Photograph: Facebook Official account of Kyrylo Budano/AFP/Getty Images Ukraine Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky Humanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city near Kherson where people have faced months of severe shortages Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.13 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war. The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children. The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine. The localised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region allowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible. View image in fullscreen Russian military personnel pass by damaged vehicles during a de-mining operation near Oleshky. Photograph: Russian Defence Ministry/Reuters Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to the southern Russian city of Anapa. “From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he added. While Ukrainian territory lies just 5km from Oleshky, evacuees will instead need to travel to Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region. “At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky,” Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post. Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky. While earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled on the convoy. View image in fullscreen The convoy carrying more than 500 evacuees from Oleshky. Photograph: Reuters Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay. Asked about whether she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a video showed a woman, who identified herself Anna, saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.” With about 2,000 people remaining in Oleshky, according to authorities and volunteers, people have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water. View image in fullscreen People in Oleshky have endured months of food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation. Photograph: The Office Of The Commissioner For Human Rights In The Russia/EPA Some say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added. “We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in images broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.” ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky Read more Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city. “They are currently checking empty houses and, in some cases, moving into them,” she told the Associated Press. “They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine,” she added. The convoy arrived under a ceasefire in the area, which the US first lady, Melania Trump, claimed to have helped broker – a rare example of cooperation between the warring sides. On Friday, the Kremlin, however, described it as a special case that was “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for a peace settlement. Oleshky was seized by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It has suffered extensive damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the huge upriver Kakhovka dam in June 2023. “The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova. View image in fullscreen Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets (centre), and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova (left), talk to journalists before the evacuation. Photograph: Office of the Ukrainian Ombudsman/AFP/Getty Images “I’ve been told that ‌it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.” He added: “This is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established across such an extensive stretch of the frontline and has been maintained for ​such a significant duration.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
